source.title: V-DEAL: Diagnosing Video Safety De-Calibration as an Understanding-Refusal Coupling Failure
source.authors: Zhe-Tong Zhang; Honghao Fu; Miao Xu; Yi-Wei Wang; Yu-Jun Cai

record.tranche_reason: Extends refusal-direction analysis to video-capable models and tests whether directions learned from external safety data transfer to video-conditioned responses. It does not reproduce the original harmful-minus-harmless direction intervention.
record.gate_note: The study measures projections onto layer-specific refusal-versus-other directions and their transfer to video responses, but does not ablate or add the original direction or edit weights. The video-aware prompt intervention deliberately induces safer responses and is not evidence about the direction itself. Layer-selection scores are used to choose layers and are not recorded as outcome rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses a difference-in-means 'refusal direction' only as a diagnostic probe. It is built from refusal vs. other response states, not harmful vs. harmless instructions. The study never ablates or adds the direction and never edits weights, so it does not test mediation (V1/V2). The transfer audit measures probe separability (ROC-AUC) from external text and image-text data to video-conditioned responses. That is cross-modality, cross-dataset detection, not transfer across languages, model variants or base-to-instruct (V6). It is also a classifier-quality score rather than evidence that the direction carries refusal. These findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that the VH-BQ vulnerability is not explained by weak video understanding alone: models recognise harmful content (over 81% accuracy; about 90% harmful-intent match), yet visual evidence yields weaker refusal-related internal signals than harmful text. A training-free prompt realignment cuts average VH-BQ ASR from 48.33% to 0.80%, comparable to fine-tuning baselines.
record.recipe_differences: The study learns normalized, layer-specific difference-in-means directions for Refusal versus Other using external safety data, ranks layers by external-corpus ROC-AUC, and averages projections from the top four layers at the last text token. It does not use the harmful-minus-harmless instruction direction or perform ablation/addition.
record.method_sensitivity: Directions and selected layers are model-specific; top m is fixed at 4, and the last text-token hidden state is used. The study says absolute projection-score scales are model-dependent. Some models have few positive refusal examples and wider transfer-AUC confidence intervals.

fits_no_version.finding: A refusal-vs-other difference-in-means probe learned on external text and image-text safety data separates refusal responses on video-conditioned inputs in all six Video LLMs. AUC is 0.85–0.96 (Refusal vs. Other) and 0.81–0.94 (Refusal vs. Harmful), above the random-direction 95th percentile.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A linear refusal-state direction estimated from text and image-text data transfers to video-conditioned inputs as a detector of refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: Harmful video with a benign query yields lower refusal rates (14.22% vs 53.05% on average) and higher ASR (48.33% vs 35.84%) than the same video with a harmful query. The pattern holds in five of six models; MiniCPM-V-4.5 is the exception.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Video LLMs under-refuse harmful visual evidence when the text query is superficially benign.

fits_no_version.finding: Projection onto the refusal probe is usually lower for VH-BQ than for T-HQ. For both Qwen models, VH-BQ falls even below T-BQ.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful visual evidence activates refusal-related representations more weakly than explicit harmful text (correlational, not causal).

record.problems: The study does not causally manipulate the direction, so its projection and transfer results cannot show that this direction mediates refusal. Projection scores are model-scale-dependent and use selected layers and a last-token representation rather than all positions. The behavioural outcomes use an LLM judge. The paper notes relatively few positive refusal examples and wider bootstrap intervals for some transfer estimates. No post-intervention general-capability check is reported for a direction intervention.
record.rows_left_out: The six T-BQ condition-level projection-score rows from Appendix Table 10 are omitted to stay within the 60-row limit while retaining transfer results, the T-HQ and video-condition projection comparisons, model-level behavioural outcomes, and reported behavioural averages. Figure 6's individual model-by-condition risk-bin values are not extracted because the figure text is flattened; the accompanying qualitative statement is not separately rowed.

untested.parts: No ablation, no addition, no harmful-minus-harmless instruction direction, no capability check.
No analysis of whether jailbreaks suppress the direction; no adversarial training.
No test of single vs. multiple directions or cone/affine structure.
Harmful-intent recognition is measured behaviourally, not as a separate internal encoding from refusal.
No cross-language, cross-variant or base-to-instruct transfer; the modality transfer is probe AUC only.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V6 'supports' label is removed. The paper's direction is a probe of refusal response states (refusal vs. other), not the original harmful-minus-harmless instruction direction. It is used for detection and scoring, never intervened on. Its cross-modality transfer is not one of V6's named transfer types. The paper cites Arditi et al. [39] as related work only.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-minus-harmless direction, all-layer/all-position ablation, direction addition, or post-intervention capability assessment.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration.
No attack that suppresses the refusal direction, or training against its ablation.
Layer-specific axes are measured, but the study does not test whether refusal is better explained by an affine set, cone, or multiple directions.
The study evaluates harmful-intent recognition and refusal-related scores, but does not test whether harmfulness judgment and refusal decision are separately encoded.
Tests transfer from external text and image-text safety data to video-conditioned responses. Does not test transfer across languages, model variants as such, or base-to-instruct models.
No comparison of refusal-training methods, timing, or training stages.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: External text and image-text refusal directions evaluated on video-conditioned responses across the six tested models
reader_labels.reason: For both transfer tasks, each reported learned-direction AUC exceeds its random-direction 95th-percentile reference; see TR01–TR12. This supports external-to-video transfer, not the untested language, model-variant, or base-to-instruct cases.
